paper_title: FMT: Lossless Image Compression in a Fixed Number of Parallel Steps

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learned lossless codecs make smaller files than common classical codecs, yet the images we archive and train on still use classical codecs. A main reason is time: a learned codec takes seconds to decode a photo that a classical codec opens in milliseconds, and their faster variants give up most of their gain in size. We argue that much of this time is spent waiting, not computing: the network waits for the values it conditions on, and the arithmetic decoder reads them one at a time. We introduce FMT (Fixed-step Multiscale Tree), a lossless image format whose decoding order and entropy coder are designed together so that neither wait grows with the image. FMT stores an image as a coarse-to-fine tree whose steps hold independent values: a GPU predicts each step at once and decodes it in parallel rANS lanes that carry their states from step to step, so an image of any size decodes in a fixed number of sequential steps. On this tree we build a family of bit-exact codecs, from a rule with no network to large networks, and no codec we ran on the same GPU beats any of them on both size and speed. Without a network, FMT beats NVIDIA's HTJ2K on size and speed; with a large one, it decodes Kodak photos 9 to 61X faster than learned codecs we ran on the same A100, at the same size or smaller.

Introduction Many images must be stored without losing single pixel: originals in archives, frames in editing pipelines, and the training data of models that restore images. Such images are written once and read many times, so how fast they decode matters as much as how small they are. Classical lossless codecs, such as PNG, JPEG-LS, JPEG XL and HTJ2K, predict or transform pixels with hand-designed rules [2, 11, 51, 60, 63] and decode photo in milliseconds. Learned codecs replace these rules with neural networks and make clearly smaller files [4, 27, 28, 33, 68], but they take seconds per photo, tens to hundreds of times longer  (Fig. 4)  , and their faster designs give up most of the gain in size [23, 28]. One must still choose between size and speed. Why are learned codecs so slow? We argue that much of their time goes to waiting rather than computing (Tab. 1). Second, the arithmetic decoder reads one value after another, often on the CPU. FNLIC [69] reports 13 ms of network inference per photo, yet in our runs it took half second per photo, two fifths of it in such coder; LCFDNet [43] took second, fifth of it in its coder on the CPU. No number of GPU cores shortens this chain (Fig. 1a). In FMT, every pixel is the end of path from coarse root (Fig. 1b), as every weight is in state trees [3]: each level adds the pixels halfway between those already decoded, predicts them from their decoded neighbours and stores only correction (the residual), so neighbouring pixels share the top of their paths, the coarser pixels they are predicted from. Each correction is in turn binarised into short path of decisions: its size, then its bits. This tree is what lets the decoder run in parallel. pixel depends only on pixels of earlier steps, so the values of one step do not depend on each other: the GPU predicts them all at once, and interleaved streams of rANS [12, 14], fast entropy coder, which we call lanes, decode their corrections in parallel, each lane carrying its state from one step to the next. Coarse-to-fine orders have long been used in image coding [22, 25, 44]; what we add is an entropy coder designed together with the order, with lanes sized by the image, not by the step as in vectorised ANS [55], so that neither link of the chain grows with the image. Since the roots spacing is fixed in pixels, photo of any size decodes in at most 72 steps, and no lane decodes more than set number of values (Tab. 1): the depth is fixed, though larger photo has larger steps. The tree also hosts classical and learned lossless coding in one format. It fixes which values are decoded together, but not how each is predicted or how its path is paid for, so hand-designed rules and neural networks become modes of the same format: fast mode stores the corrections of reversible wavelet at fixed widths, with no entropy coder; dense mode predicts each pixel by the mean of four neighbours and codes the paths with histograms learned once, with no network; and neural modes, with networks from 16 neurons in 2 layers (162) to 768 in 4 (7684), give every possible correction its own probability, and the encoder tunes them to each photo. All decode bit-exactly on the GPU, and on other GPU types with our portable kernels. Across this family, no codec we ran on the same GPU beats any FMT mode on both size and speed, on Kodak or on two sets of large photos (Fig. 4 and Tab. 3). Without network, FMT beats NVIDIAs HTJ2K in both size and speed. With small network, it makes smaller files than JPEG XL and decodes them faster on one GPU than JPEG XL does on 32-thread CPU. With large network, it decodes Kodak photo 9 to 61 faster than the learned codecs we ran from their authors code on an A100, at the same size or smaller (Tab. 4). At full load, the fast mode decodes more pixels per second than any other codec we ran (Tab. 6). In summary, we make three contributions: 1. Where the time of learned lossless decoding goes. Profiles of three released codecs, and our own networks decoded with longer coder chains or more steps, show that much of it goes to waiting, not computing (Sec. 4.4, Sec. S6.6). 2. decoding schedule whose sequential work does not grow with the image. The order and the entropy coder are designed together: coarse-to-fine tree of corrections, each short path of decisions, fixes the number of steps by its roots spacing, and rANS lanes whose number grows with the image carry their states across steps, so prediction and entropy decoding both run in parallel on the GPU. Neither half suffices alone: with one coder, the same order still takes most of second [22]; with fresh lanes at every step, files grow by up to 14% (about 24% in the dense mode; Secs. 3.1, 3.2, 3.4 and 3.5, Sec. GPU decoders for every mode, portable kernels whose streams decode alike on different GPUs (also with 8-bit tensor-core layers) and CPU decoders, compared from compressed bytes to verified pixels with classical codecs on one GPU and one CPU and with learned codecs run from their authors code, including where they still win (Secs. 4 and 5). 2. Related work Lossless coding as prediction. Most lossless codecs predict each pixel from decoded neighbours and code the residual: CALIC [63] and LOCO-I, the core of JPEG-LS [60], in raster order with fixed predictors and adaptive contexts; PNG [11], WebP [64] and QOI [50] with simpler rules; FLIF [48] and JPEG XL [2, 49] with context tree learned for each image; GraLIC [42] mixes many predictors per pixel, far more slowly. JPEG 2000 [52] decorrelates the image with reversible integer wavelet [7], and HTJ2K [51] 2 codes it with high-throughput block coder. Coarse-to-fine orders are old: hierarchical interpolation [44, 46] predicts from coarser grids, Kim and Cho [25] pair such hierarchy with context-adaptive arithmetic coding, much as our dense mode does, and FLIFs interlaced mode, PNGs Adam7 [11] and JPEG XLs Squeeze [49] decode coarse to fine. Learned lossless codecs. PixelCNN [47, 56] runs network per value. Later codecs predict groups of values: multiand subscale models [32, 41, 65], hierarchical latents (L3C [33], SHVC [45]), super-resolution (SReC [8]), frequency bands (LC-FDNet [43]), lossy plus residual (RC [34], DLPR [4]) and bit planes (ArIB-BPS [68]). Integer flows [18, 59, 66, 67], probabilistic circuits [31], per-image fitting (FNLIC [69], and for lossy coding Cool-chic [26] and C3 [24]) and adaptation (CALLIC [27]) differ; checkerboard contexts [16, 17] decode lossy latents in two steps. Making learned codecs fast. The attempt most similar to FMT is Kamislis interpolation codec [22], which stores sparse grid of pixels and predicts the finer grids from coarser ones with small networks: essentially our decoding order. Its network runs only about 15 times per image, yet it still takes most of second per photo by its paper, because single arithmetic coder on the CPU decodes every value in turn. HPAC [28] bounds its network steps by working on patches and comes closest to our largest networks in size, but by its paper it takes about second per Kodak photo, 17 times as long as our 5124. PILC [23] takes the opposite route: it runs entirely on the GPU and is fast, but its files are about as large as WebPs, which our dense mode, without any network, beats in both size and throughput (Tab. 6). Wavefront codecs [6, 15] decode many pixels at once, DLIC [6] with rANS on the GPU, but in steps whose number grows with the image (Sec. 4.4). Together they show that parallel order alone does not make decoding fast, and that speed bought with simple model gives up the size. For lossy video, DCVC-RT [20] finds speed limited by operations other than computation and trims them in its network; FMT instead bounds the number of sequential steps. What FMT adds is an entropy coder designed together with its order: the values of each step are spread over interleaved rANS lanes that carry their states from step to step, and the predictors are cheap enough per step, with integer probabilities, to keep both prediction and entropy decoding on the GPU, bit-exact. Three ways to code the tree An entropy coder turns each value into bits according to the probability the decoder will give it: value of probability costs about log2 bits, so the better the probabilities, the smaller the file. The encoder and the decoder must therefore compute the same probabilities from what is already decoded. Classical codecs do this by counting: they sort values into few contexts, classes of similar neighbourhoods, and code each value with the histogram of its context [60, 63]. Learned codecs instead let network compute the probability of every possible value from the neighbourhood [33, 47]. 4 Both hand their probabilities to an entropy coder such as rANS [12], whose decoder keeps one integer state and reads each value by finding where that state falls in the values cumulative distribution. FMT offers both kinds, and third that needs no probabilities at all (Tab. 2). The tree fixes which values are decoded together; the modes decide how each value is predicted and how its path is paid for. Dense: shared histograms. The dense mode follows the classical recipe on the pixel tree. It predicts each new pixel by the rounded mean of its four nearest decoded neighbours  (Fig. 2)  and codes the first decisions of each correction, its size and the bit after its leading one, with rANS under histogram; the remaining bits, close to uniform, are coded at uniform probability. The histogram depends on context made of two values: how much the four neighbours differ, and how large their corrections were, there and in the previous colour channel. Similar neighbourhoods have similar histograms in every image, so one codebook of 256 histograms, learned once on training photos, serves all images, and file stores only which histogram each of its contexts uses. Decoding value takes few integer operations and no network. Its limit is the context: two hand-chosen values can tell only so many neighbourhoods apart. Neural: learned probabilities. The neural modes remove that limit by replacing the context and its histogram with network that computes the probability of every possible correction from the neighbourhood itself. For each value, small multilayer perceptron reads the nearest decoded pixels, relative to the mean of the nearest four, which remains the prediction; how much these four differ; and, in the second and third colour channels, the values already decoded at and around the same pixel. One-hot inputs tell it the level and the kind of step, so one network per colour channel serves the whole tree. It outputs mixture of discretised logistics [47], smooth distribution over all corrections, which the encoder and the decoder turn into the same integer table for rANS (Sec. 3.4). The network only prices each correction: weaker one makes larger file, never wrong pixel. The networks are trained to minimise the code length of the corrections on crops of training photos. For more context, the neural modes split each step in two, so the second half also sees the first: the centres in two checkerboard halves, the edges as horizontal, then vertical midpoints. This fixes the number of steps, not the time: larger image has larger steps. Lanes that carry their state. An rANS decoder is sequential: it reads one value after another from its stream. To decode many values at once, the stream is interleaved: the values are dealt to many lanes, each separate rANS decoder with its own state, run by one GPU thread [14]. FMT deals the values of every step to the lanes in turn, and each lane keeps its state from one step to the next. The number of lanes therefore follows the size of the image, not of the step: an image gets enough lanes that each decodes about values in all, lane length that trades parallelism against the few bytes of each lanes final state (Tab. 2). Giving each step lanes of its own would need many times as many lanes for the same chain length, each with final state to store, and make files 13% larger with our 162 (Sec. S3.3). Bit-exact probabilities. Lossless decoding needs the decoder to compute exactly the same probabilities as the encoder: single difference in rounding makes it read wrong value, and the error spreads to every value predicted from it. Floating-point results depend on the order of operations, which compilers, libraries and GPUs may change. We therefore turn each networks mixture into an integer cumulative distribution, with fixed-point arithmetic and table of the sigmoid, in which every value keeps nonzero frequency (Sec. S5.1), and our kernels fix the order of every operation. The dense and fast modes compute with integers only, so any processor decodes their streams, and those of our small networks decode bit for bit on all three GPUs we tested. 3.5. Why tree? Two things decide how fast an image decodes and how small its file is: how many steps must run one after another, and how much of the decoded image each value can see. The tree trades little of the second for much of the first (Tab. 1). Few steps. In raster order, every value waits for the one before it; in the tree, only the steps wait for each other, and the lanes keep each decoders chain short. The lanes are not tied to the tree: any order that decodes groups of values could use them. What the tree adds is that these groups stay few and large for an image of any size, because its root is so sparse that storing it costs almost nothing. Context on all sides. Most pixels see more in the tree than in raster order: the three quarters of the pixels that the last level adds have decoded neighbours on all four sides, where raster order offers only those above and to the left. The price is paid at the coarse levels, whose decoded neighbours are far away: their values cost about twice the bits, but the first three levels hold under 2% of values. Only general-purpose formats with much larger files decode faster than our fast mode, and only learned codecs that take tens of times longer make smaller files: HPAC-FT and CALLIC on Kodak, and DLPR and ArIB-BPS on DIV2K, by 0.7 and 1.0%. HTJ2K, decoded by NVIDIAs library, on both axes and on every dataset: its files are 810% smaller, it decodes photo 1.21.6 faster (1.11.4 with faster host CPU; Sec. S7.4), and, with longer lanes, it stays smaller and faster at full load (Tab. 6). It is 914 faster than JPEG 2000 on the same GPU, at the same size or smaller. Against JPEG XL. At effort 9, the highest we ran on all three datasets, JPEG XL (libjxl 0.11.2) is the strongest classical codec in our comparison. Tuned to each photo, as JPEG XL learns context tree for each, our 642 network makes files 2.33.8% smaller, smaller on 45 of the 49 Kodak and DIV2K/4 photos (Tab. Design choices Decoding order. To see what the tree costs, we train the same networks for 2:1 wavefront, the most parallel order in which value sees its left, upper and upper-right neighbours (Sec. S3.4). Our 162 and 642 then gain 1.6% on Kodak (files) and 2.4% (tuned code length), but the gain does not grow with capacity: 5124 trained both ways with short recipe gains nothing once tuned. The wavefront, however, takes 78 times as many steps, number that grows with the image: about 24,000 for 4K frame, where the tree still takes 72 (our 162 decodes one in 33 ms, Sec. S3.4). Our kernels, built for few large steps, decode the wavefront 40 slower; decoder built for small steps would narrow this gap, but synchronising its steps alone would take as long as our 162s whole decode. Tiles stop the steps from growing, but not the cost of having many (Fig. 5, Sec. S3.4). Inside tiles of 64 pixels, the most parallel choice, the wavefront still takes 567 steps, 8 the trees: with the same encoder and kernels, its 162 makes files 0.3% smaller than ours at 4.6 the decode time (its 642: 0.8%, in tuned code length), and our 642 is 4.5% smaller in less than half that time. The tree thus trades 0.3 to 2.4% of size for 8 to 78 fewer steps. Root, lanes and tuning. root every 32 or 128 pixels instead of 64 changes the code length by at most 0.5% (Sec. S3.5), and single warp of lanes instead of 18 makes files only 0.4% smaller and every network over 20 ms slower 8 (Sec. S3.2), 0.65 µs for each value lane decodes in turn: the second link of the chain, measured with the networks unchanged. Per-photo tuning saves 3.76.7% on Kodak, against 0.30.7% for the colour transforms and orientations, and still pays on 64 64 crops (Secs. S4.1, S4.5). 5. Limitations FMT is built for 8-bit photos written once and read many times. Tuning to each photo takes seconds on the GPU, 3.58.9 per Kodak photo with our 5124 on an A100 (HPAC-FT: 8.45 [28]) and 214 per 2K photo with our fastest encoders (Sec. S4.4), and on CPU, FMT is competitive only one image at time. Our decoder keeps tables and buffers for each image size, 276403 bytes per pixel, up to 9.6 GB for 33-megapixel image (Sec. S7.1), or none if rebuilt per image (+1.5 ms, Sec. S7.3), and 64 64 thumbnail still takes the 72 steps: 3.2 ms with our 162, against about 0.5 ms for CPU codecs (Sec. S4.5). The best codecs that adapt to each image remain 1.83.4% smaller on the full sets. Our 1282 and larger networks have no CPU decoder yet, and their portable kernels cost time: 3.04.4 in fp32, or up to 1.2 with 8-bit layers (RTX 3090, 4090), for files at most 0.25% larger (Secs. S5.3S5.4). Images of 10 to 16 bits (film masters, medical scans) need networks trained on them and wider frequency tables; we tested photographs only. Files need checksums: errors spread to finer levels. 6. Conclusion Our results suggest that much of the time learned lossless codecs take can go to sequential work rather than to their networks. coarse-to-fine schedule designed with its entropy coder bounds this work, to few dozen steps and set number of values per lane, for an image of any size. On such trees, from quarter of millisecond to tens of milliseconds per photo, codec without network beats HTJ2K on both axes, small networks reach the file sizes of some learned codecs at classical speed, and our largest networks spend their decode mostly on arithmetic, not on entropy decoding.

The main papers Tab. 2 sets the three modes side by side. Algorithm S1 summarises the GPU decoder of the pixel-tree modes (main paper, Sec. 3.4). Phase 1 runs one thread per value of step; phase 2 runs one thread per lane, lane of warp g, and the warps of the image keep their lanes rANS states from step to step. The slot is the low 16 bits of lanes state. In the dense mode, phase 1 computes the prediction and the context of each value, and phase 2 looks up its histogram and decodes the remaining bits of large corrections at uniform probability, through the same state. Training The 162 to 642 train for 60,000 steps at peak learning rate of 2 103, then for 120,000 more at 103; the 1282 only for the first 60,000, which is why we did not time it on the large photos. The 5124 trains in three cycles, the last of 80,000 steps at peak learning rate of 5 104; the 12 7684 is the 5124 after its second cycle, widened without changing its function, then trained for the same third cycle. All train on the same 25,834 crops of 512 512 pixels: grid over the DIV2K [1] training images and random crops of the CLIC [54] and Flickr2K [29] training images, none of them test image. Per-photo tuning runs Adam at learning rate of 103 on cosine schedule. The lane runs of this section and the encoder runs of Sec. S4 encode and decode the 24 Kodak photos on one RTX 3090 (CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.11), the GPU of our CPU machine, one image at time, and every one of their decodes equals the photo bit for bit. Portable kernels variant of our kernels removes both causes (Tab. S11). It replaces the approximate exponential, in the SiLU and in the mixtures weights and scales, by one of its own (CodyWaite reduction and degree-6 polynomial in fused multiplyadds, within about one ulp) and the one logarithm, of an integer from 1 to 511, by table; and it runs the layers of the 1282 to 7684 in fp32, in kernel of its own in which every output is the bias plus the products summed in increasing order of the inner index, one fused multiplyadd each, whatever the tiling. Every result is then defined by correctly rounded IEEE-754 operations in fixed order. The encoder and the decoder both use these kernels, so the streams change, by at most 0.005% in size.
